PR #364 activates the Avengers arsenal: local runtime discovery, callability

guard. Merged whole -- nothing removed.

Exercised rather than only tested, and the chain has a reporting defect. It is
doctor -> plan -> tick, each step reading what the last one wrote, and all four
input paths threw into a generic handler that printed the raw error:

  AVENGERS_TICK_CRASHED / ENOENT: no such file or directory, open

That is the arsenal's most common state on this host, and it is not a crash.
Nothing is callable without a configured provider, so the planner correctly
refuses with no-callable-avenger for every node and writes no plan. The system
working as designed was being reported as a filesystem error about a filename.

A missing artifact now names the step that has not run, the command that
produces it, and -- this is the part that matters -- that the producing step may
itself legitimately refuse. Without that last clause an operator reads the
refusal as a second bug and goes looking for it. A malformed artifact is
distinguished from an absent one and says regenerate rather than repair by hand,
because a half-written artifact is worse than none: everything downstream would
treat whatever parsed as truth.

AVENGERS-INPUT-01 and -02 kill both halves. The second had to be re-anchored:
mutating `JSON.parse(text)` to `JSON.parse(text) || {}` changes no output for
any valid object, so it survived every test -- unfalsifiable rather than
untested. Anchored on the refusal branch, it kills.

Fix the four tests main is shipping red

Compared failure sets rather than assuming: origin/main fails 24 tests, this
branch failed 7, and every one of the 7 was also red on main. Nothing here was
caused by the merge. Three were the canon figures; these are the other four.

**The autonomy followup could never pass.** The receipt ledger needs store.add
and store.get, and the test's fake store had neither, so the job refused with
store-atomic-add-and-get-required. The refusal is correct -- an execution receipt
is written under a deterministic id precisely so a duplicate tick cannot write a
second one, and a store that cannot refuse the duplicate cannot provide that.
The fake now models the real one: add throws on a repeated id, get returns what
is there. A fake that accepted every add would let a double-write pass here and
fail in production.

**The model admission fixture had no provider**, and the module requires one, so
that test also arrived red and stayed red. The requirement is the half worth
keeping: an admission that cannot name who served the model is exactly what the
routing law exists to refuse, since fallback must preserve provider identity in
receipts. Fixture repaired, and the gap it was hiding given its own test.

**The brain's capability count was pinned at 8 and the registry now holds 11.**
Updated rather than loosened -- registering a supplier should arrive as a failing
test rather than as three more capabilities nobody decided on, and this
assertion is what said so. The three new ids are named individually, so a
supplier cannot be swapped for another without saying so.

Test the recovery lock instead of hoping two workers overlap

The Gmail concurrency test started two recovery workers with Promise.all and
asserted that exactly one claimed the row. On a fast disposable database they
stopped overlapping, both claimed it, and the test failed.

Both claims were legitimate. RESULT_UNCERTAIN is itself an unresolved status, so
once the first worker commits the row back to RESULT_UNCERTAIN it is a valid
candidate again -- and nothing was double-dispatched, which is the invariant
that actually matters. "Exactly one worker claims it" was never true of
sequential runs. A concurrency test that depends on losing a race proves nothing
on the days it wins one, and the file's own comment had already talked itself
into believing the both-claimed branch was "excluded by PostgreSQL semantics".

So the overlap is made real rather than hoped for: the first worker's
transaction is held open, and the second must find nothing to claim while it is.
That is FOR UPDATE SKIP LOCKED being tested rather than assumed, and
RECOVERY-LOCK-01 now kills its removal.

Three smaller things fell out of proving it can fail:

- The dispatch-count assertion folded in the adapter that performed the original
  authorized dispatch, whose count is 1 by design, so it would have passed or
  failed for the wrong reason. Counted on the recovery worker now, with the
  original dispatch asserted separately as exactly one.
- The holder is released in a finally. It was released after the assertion, so a
  failure left the holder's transaction parked and pool.end() waiting on it --
  the suite stalled instead of reporting the failure it had just found.
- lock_timeout and statement_timeout are set per connection rather than through
  the `options` connection parameter, which was tried first and silently did
  nothing. A timeout that is not in force looks like protection and is worse
  than none.

Run the transition-guard check inside the server instead of across the wire

The exhaustive (from,to) check walked 132 pairs from the client -- BEGIN, an
insert, a few updates, ROLLBACK -- roughly six hundred round trips. On this
container that is not merely slow. Around the 122nd transaction the connection
stops responding: the backend sits `active`, waits on nothing, holds no lock and
ignores statement_timeout, because it is blocked writing a result to a socket.
Nothing times it out from either side, so the suite stopped rather than failed.

Three isolation fixes were tried and none of them moved it -- a pool, then one
dedicated client, then a fresh connection per pair, each stopping in the same
place. That is what identified the cost as the round trips themselves rather
than anything held in a session or a pool, and it is why the earlier diagnosis
("the pool was empty after roughly 120 of the 132 pairs") was wrong about the
mechanism while being right about where it stopped.

The loop now runs in PL/pgSQL: four statements instead of six hundred. Each
attempt gets its own subtransaction so a rejection rolls that pair back, and an
accepted row is deleted afterwards because the partial unique index on
business_key is part of what is under test. Only the attempt is guarded -- a
failure while walking the legal setup path is a broken fixture, not a verdict,
so it fails loudly rather than being recorded as a rejection the database never
made.

The check is stronger than before, not weaker: the client no longer takes any
part in deciding what the database accepted. Falsified before being believed --
claiming every transition is legal fails with Postgres's own message, "illegal
execution transition: <new> -> DISPATCHING".

Also removes an unref that was masking this. It stopped a stuck socket pinning
the event loop, but with nothing else pending the loop drained mid-query and the
runner cancelled the test with "Promise resolution is still pending but the
event loop has already resolved" -- deterministically, every run. A socket must
be a reason to stay alive while the test runs and stop being one when it ends:
that is a destroy in the finally, not an unref at the top.

Break the hang cascade, and take one bounded second look at a hang

Three guards -- HYG-01, HYG-02, MONEY-17 -- kept reporting SUITE_TIMED_OUT in a
full run and KILLED alone. The failing set drifted later each run, which is the
signature of a cascade rather than three unreliable tests.

A suite killed at its deadline can leave a PostgreSQL backend that never notices
its client is gone: the stall the postgres-real runner already documents. Each
one holds a connection and keeps working, so the first hang in a run makes the
next one likelier. Those clients are provably gone -- the runner killed the
process that opened them -- so they are terminated before each database-backed
mutation, reclaiming the connection rather than interrupting live work.

With the cascade cut, a hang can still happen, and a guard that was never tested
is the one thing this file must not leave standing. So a SUITE_TIMED_OUT gets
one second attempt, against the reclaimed state rather than as a repeat of an
unchanged mechanism.

This is deliberately not "retry until it passes":
- only a hang qualifies, because that is the verdict meaning no measurement was
  taken. A SURVIVED or a KILLED is a measurement and stands on the first run.
- exactly one attempt, no loop.
- whatever it finds is recorded, including another hang.
- the row is printed as "(second attempt after a hang)", so it can never be read
  as a clean first pass.

A test asserts that shape rather than leaving it to review, because a retry loop
is how a mutation gate quietly stops meaning anything.

Bound the mutation war's suites, and stop journaling skips

Two defects, both found by the war stalling in front of me.

**No suite deadline.** The war ran each killing suite with no timeout, so one
suite that never returned left the whole run in ep_poll with no output, no
verdict, and nothing to say which mutation it was on -- thirteen minutes of a
run went that way before anyone read /proc. A real database makes that hang
reachable, which the postgres-real runner already found the hard way; the war
never got the same repair.

Each test is now bounded at 120s so most hangs surface as an ordinary failure,
with a 600s wall deadline as the backstop for a suite wedged before the runner
starts counting. A killed suite gets its own verdict: SUITE_TIMED_OUT, which
lands in "not tested at all" and fails the run rather than being absorbed into
KILLED or SURVIVED. It dominates the exit code deliberately -- a suite killed
mid-run can emit a partial TAP stream carrying a failure count, which would
otherwise read as a mutant that died when nothing finished.

**Skips were journaled.** SKIPPED_NEEDS_POSTGRES says this host had no database.
That is a fact about the machine, not a judgement about the guard, and replaying
it into a later run on a machine that has one would report a capability gap that
no longer exists and quietly stop testing that guard for good -- the same shape
as the CRAWL-01 problem the browser resolver was written to end, arriving
through the mechanism built to fix it.

The rule lives in appendVerdict rather than at the call site, because it is the
journal's invariant and a caller that forgets it should not be able to write
one. Everything else survives, including the bad news: SURVIVED, SUITE_TIMED_OUT
and ANCHOR_AMBIGUOUS are all remembered, or the record could only ever improve.

TIMEOUT-01 and JOURNAL-03 kill both. JOURNAL-03's anchor had to move into
mutation-journal.mjs for the same self-reference reason as the browser resolver:
an anchor quoted in the registry that lives in the registry's own file matches
twice.

Make the mutation war survive being interrupted

The full war takes over an hour against a real database, and this host restarts
its container under load. Four consecutive runs were killed in flight, each one
discarding every verdict it had already earned, so the summary line the
readiness artifact quotes had never once been produced for the current registry.
Restarting it hopefully a fifth time is not a plan.

MUTATION_WAR_JOURNAL appends each verdict the moment it is decided and replays
it on the next run, so an interrupted war resumes instead of starting over.
Replayed rows are labelled in the output; a run that says KILLED should be able
to say whether it watched that happen.

A resumable gate is also a gate that can report work nobody did, so the binding
is the feature rather than a detail. Every entry carries a hash of the mutation
that earned it -- file, anchor, replacement and killing suites. Move any of
them and the entry stops matching and the mutation runs again, because a verdict
is about a specific guard in a specific place, not about an id. Suite order is
deliberately not part of it: a cosmetic reordering should not discard an hour of
real evidence, or the resume is one nobody uses.

Five tests hold this down, because its failure mode is a green summary line
rather than a red one, and a green lie is not something a later run corrects:
an id alone cannot claim a verdict, a wrong or absent fingerprint is refused, a
damaged journal loses entries rather than inventing them, a missing journal is
empty rather than an error, and a later verdict supersedes an earlier one in
both directions -- a SURVIVED recorded after a KILLED must stick, or the record
can only ever improve. JOURNAL-01 and JOURNAL-02 confirm both halves are killed
when weakened.

that was chosen but not defended is a rule the next merge can quietly choose
differently, so each one now has something that fails when it goes.

Ten mutations, covering what this merge actually settled:

- CONV-01 caller-asserted provider state cannot open a LIVE route
- CONV-02 the gateway reads AI_GATEWAY_*, never a prefix derived from its id
- CONV-03/04 negative rates and unparseable verification dates are not pricing
- CONV-05 a record this system generated cannot verify itself
- CONV-06 the fifth qualified conversation with no paid pilot ends the canary
- CONV-07 the first-cash offer stays bound to the canonical Lead-Path SKU
- CONV-08 CODE_READY needs observed operation, not an absence of complaints
- POSTAL-409 a 409 is ambiguous, never a definite rejection
- POSTAL-ZERO no webhook row is not proof that nothing was submitted

138 registered mutations become 148, and every anchor resolves to exactly one
site.

The hostile suite attacks nine ways a caller could get a stronger answer than
the evidence supports. Two of them found nothing because the protection already
held, so both were verified by removing the protection and watching the test
fail: dropping the unowned-assignment refusal lets `send.attacker.example` be
planned under an owned root, and restoring the convergence stub's
`if (gaps.length) overall = 'DISTRIBUTION_BLOCKED'` lets an unfinished module
hide a missing credential. A green sweep that survives deleting the guard is not
evidence.

Also closed here, all four verified failing on a clean worktree of acc7d132
first:

- The customer-binding fixture now carries the cleared-payment stage reference,
  the canonical product and the three-witness boundary its validator demands.
  The validator was right; the fixture was three requirements behind it.
- DomainDNSError is no longer asserted to prove a message was submitted. It is
  an event about the sending domain's records, it can arrive when nothing was
  ever sent, and reading it as acceptance would let a domain-wide
  misconfiguration certify a send that never happened. It reconciles to
  UNCERTAIN, and the adapter's own status set already agreed.
- Three modules main merged with no entry point are resolved: the canary guard
  by wiring it, and the Genome admission step and proposal engine by classifying
  them against gates that state what would release them.
- Three mutation anchors that pointed into the replaced files now point at the
  equivalent guards in the versions that survived.

Security audit of the changed surface: no shell-interpolating subprocess call,
no fetch on a caller-supplied URL, 0 dependency vulnerabilities. The Postal
route refuses before reading when unconfigured, caps the body at 1 MiB before
parsing, verifies over exact bytes, declines to reinterpret Postal's legacy
SHA-1 header as SHA-256, and answers a storage failure without echoing the
connection string. Sender evidence can only be applied by an authenticated DNS
event and only pauses, never enables.

Merge main and the night convergence harvest, resolved by verified semantics

Both lanes built the same six capabilities under different names. The merge
picked per file by what each version actually protects, not by which branch was
newer or larger.

Main's work wins where it is genuinely stronger:

- The Postal evidence layer handles DomainDNSError sender evidence, rejects
  future-dated events and orders lifecycle states monotonically, none of which
  the Ragnarok version did. Its reconciliation lookup filters quarantined rows
  at the wrapper, which is a real boundary.
- The Postal adapter is v1.3.0 and already carries the dispatch timeout, the
  executionId-optional reconcile and the provenance check the Ragnarok branch
  was built to add. Only the shared-primitives refactor was unique, and it stays
  where the Gmail adapter uses it.
- lead-path-sprint-fulfillment composes the canonical service-fulfillment engine
  and binds the sprint to a SKU, a recomputed payment-truth digest and a
  provider event that may not read as sandbox or synthetic. The Ragnarok branch
  had reimplemented a parallel state machine beside it; that duplicate and its
  test are gone.
- The executor factory's single `ai-gateway` identity matches the provider list
  main's own entry-point test asserts. The Ragnarok alias would have broken it.

The convergence harvest wins on one rule and loses on four files:

- LIVE routing may no longer be opened by caller-supplied provider states. Four
  booleans anybody can type are not an activation, and the test that used to
  prove LIVE worked that way now proves it refuses, with a receipt-derived route
  beside it so the legitimate door is still shown to open. Supplying both
  receipts and states reports the ambiguity as well, which that rewrite had
  swallowed.
- Its four "harvested" doctors were 33-, 61-, 64- and 83-line stubs that take
  the answer as an argument: `softwareGaps: []` in, `CODE_READY` out. The
  measuring implementations are kept and now export the convergence names, so
  either vocabulary reaches one answer. In the classifier a software gap can no
  longer mask a credential blocker, and absent elapsed-observation proof the
  verdict is never CODE_READY.
- The rewrite had also stripped the comments explaining why observed quotas only
  tighten, why an unknown audience is refused on a capped provider and why two
  sources for one truth is ambiguity. Restored: those are the reasons someone
  needs before deciding a rule looks unnecessary.

Four reds that origin/main is shipping right now, all verified on a clean
worktree of acc7d132 before anything here was touched:

- `npm run brain`, the mandatory first command of every session, returns
  UBERBOND_BRAIN_BOOTSTRAP_FAILED because CURRENT_OWNER_DOCTRINE was never added
  to MEMORY_STATUSES.
- config/system-readiness-input.json is truncated mid-array, so canon cannot be
  regenerated at all. Restored from 60f7f6e5 with 21 capability entries a
  truncated write had dropped.
- The four customer-binding tests fail because the validator gained three
  requirements the fixture never got: the cleared-payment stage must name the
  same provider event, the product must be the canonical SKU, and the
  three-witness product boundary must be declared. The fixture was fixed, not
  the validator.
- Three modules merged with no entry point and no classification. The canary
  guard is now wired by making the packet delegate to it rather than restating
  "at most five" in a second place; the Genome admission step and the proposal
  engine are classified against gates that say what would release them.

The first-cash canary can no longer walk a rehearsal sprint, because the
canonical machine refuses synthetic payment evidence by design. It now
demonstrates that refusal instead, which is the more useful property: a canary
that could open that door would be reporting that anyone could.
